6.3  Folder Structure and Paths 
Files on a computer are organised in a hierarchical tree structure. At the top is the root (C:\ 
on Windows, / on Linux/macOS), then folders branch out from there. 
 
 
Figure 6.2 — File System Hierarchy: Folder Tree and Path Structure 
 
Example File Path: 
C:\Users\Ahmed\Documents\School\Chapter1.docx 
This means: On drive C, inside Users, inside Ahmed, inside Documents, inside School, there is 
a file called Chapter1.docx. 
 
Understanding paths is important because: 
• Every file has a unique path (location address). 
• Programs use paths to find files automatically. 
• Shortcuts use paths to link to files or programs. 
 
6.4  Using File Explorer (Windows)

6.7  Searching for Files 
When you cannot remember where a file is saved, use the search function: 
• In File Explorer: Click the search box (top right) and type the file name or part of it. 
• Windows Search: Press the Windows key and start typing. 
• Search by type: Type *.docx to find all Word documents in a folder. 
• Search by date: Use the Date Modified filter in the search options. 
 
6.8  Compressing and Extracting Files 
Compression reduces file size by encoding data more efficiently. This is useful for sending 
files by email or saving space. 
• To compress: Select files > right-click > Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder. 
• To extract: Right-click the .zip file > Extract All > choose destination folder. 
• Common formats: .zip (universal), .rar (more compression), .7z (open-source). 
 
6.9  Good File Organisation Habits 
Keeping your files well-organised saves time and prevents data loss. Follow these best 
practices: 
 
Best Practices for File Organisation 
✓ Use clear, descriptive file names (e.g., Science_Assignment_March.docx, not 
doc1.docx). 
✓ Create a logical folder structure: School > Subjects > Year > Term. 
✓ Save files in the correct folder immediately — do not leave everything in Downloads. 
✓ Back up important files regularly to an external drive or cloud storage. 
✓ Delete files you no longer need to free up storage space. 
✓ Avoid special characters (?, *, :, /, \) in file names — they cause errors.

8.1  What is Microsoft PowerPoint? 
Microsoft PowerPoint is a presentation software that allows users to create slideshows made 
up of individual slides. Each slide can contain text, images, charts, videos, and animations. 
Presentations are used in classrooms, businesses, conferences, and events to communicate 
ideas visually. 
PowerPoint files are saved with the .pptx extension. The software is part of the Microsoft 
Office / Microsoft 365 suite.

9.1  What is Microsoft Excel? 
Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet application used to organise, calculate, and analyse data. It 
is one of the most powerful and widely used business tools in the world. Excel is used for 
budgets, timetables, mark sheets, scientific data, financial analysis, and much more. 
Excel files are saved as .xlsx. They are made up of workbooks (the file) and worksheets 
(individual sheets/tabs within the file).

9.3  Understanding Cells, Rows, and Columns 
A cell is identified by its column letter followed by its row number. This is called a cell 
reference or cell address. 
• Cell A1 = Column A, Row 1 (top-left cell). 
• Cell C5 = Column C, Row 5. 
• A range of cells: A1:C5 means all cells from A1 to C5. 
• Entire column: Click the column letter (e.g., A) to select all of column A. 
• Entire row: Click the row number (e.g., 5) to select all of row 5. 
 
9.4  Entering Data 
Data Type Description 
Text (Labels) Words, names, headings. Aligned left by 
default. Example: "Name", "Subject". 
Numbers (Values) Numeric data used in calculations. Aligned right 
by default. Example: 85, 1200.50. 
Dates Excel recognises dates (e.g., 01/01/2024) and 
can perform date calculations. 
Formulas Start with = sign. Example: =A1+B1, 
=SUM(A1:A10). 
 
• Type in a cell and press Enter (move down) or Tab (move right). 
• Edit a cell: Press F2 or double-click the cell. 
• Clear a cell: Press Delete key (removes content but keeps formatting). 
 
9.5  Formatting Cells 
9.5.1  Text Formatting 
Select cells and use the Home tab for basic text formatting: Font, Size, Bold (Ctrl+B), Italic 
(Ctrl+I), Underline, Font Colour, and Fill Colour (background colour). 
9.5.2  Number Formats 
Format Example

Text Treats number as text — no calculations 
 
9.5.3  Cell Alignment and Merge

• Wrap Text: Home > Wrap Text — makes text visible on multiple lines in one cell.

Formula What it Does

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
10.1  What is the Internet? 
The Internet is a global network of billions of computers and devices connected together, 
allowing them to share information and communicate. It was originally developed in the 
1960s by the US military (ARPANET) and opened to the public in the early 1990s. 
The Internet works by breaking data into small pieces called packets, sending them through 
various routes, and reassembling them at the destination. This is called packet switching. 
 
Internet vs World Wide Web — Not the Same Thing! 
The Internet: The physical global network of cables, routers, and connections. 
The World Wide Web (WWW): A service that runs ON the Internet — a collection of web pages 
accessed through a browser. Email, online gaming, and video streaming also use the Internet 
but are not part of the Web. 
 
10.2  How the Internet Works 
 
Figure 10.1 — How the Internet Works: DNS Lookup and Data Flow 
10.2.1  IP Addresses 
Every device on the internet has a unique IP address (Internet Protocol address) — like a 
postal address for computers. 
• IPv4: Four groups of numbers (e.g., 192.168.1.1) — over 4 billion addresses. 
• IPv6: Newer format with 8 groups of hexadecimal (e.g., 2001:0db8::1) — nearly 
unlimited addresses. 
• Your home router has a public IP address. Devices in your home have private IP 
addresses. 
 
10.2.2  DNS (Domain Name System) 
Humans use domain names (e.g., www.google.com) instead of IP addresses. The DNS 
translates domain names into IP addresses automatically — like a phone book for the 
internet. 
 
82

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
10.2.3  Protocols 
Protocol Purpose 
HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol — transfers web 
pages from server to browser. 
HTTPS Secure HTTP — encrypts data between 
browser and server. Look for padlock icon. 
FTP File Transfer Protocol — transfers files between 
computers. 
SMTP / POP3 / IMAP Email protocols — sending and receiving 
messages. 
TCP/IP The foundational protocol suite of the internet 
— controls data packet routing. 
 
10.3  Understanding URLs 
 
Figure 10.2 — Anatomy of a URL: Every Part Explained 
Extension Meaning 
.com Commercial — most common, used worldwide.

.edu Educational institution. 
.gov Government website.

.co.uk UK-based company. 
.pk / .in / .de Country-code TLDs for Pakistan, India, 
Germany, etc. 
 
10.4  Web Browsers 
A web browser is software used to access and display websites. It sends requests to web 
servers and renders (displays) the HTML/CSS/JavaScript it receives.

separate tabs.

much faster than dial-up. 
Cable Broadband Uses TV cable infrastructure. Fast and 
common in homes.

Service Description 
website or app.

10.7a  Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)
A Virtual Private Network (VPN) is a security tool that creates an encrypted,
private tunnel between your device and a VPN server before your traffic reaches the
wider internet. It is an important internet service that every digital citizen
should understand.
How a VPN Works What a VPN Protects Against
1. Your device connects to
   a VPN server (encrypted).
2. VPN server makes requests
   on your behalf.
3. Websites see the VPN
   server's IP, not yours.
4. All traffic between you
   and VPN is encrypted.
· Snooping on public Wi-Fi
  (cafes, airports, hotels).
· Your ISP seeing your
  browsing history.
· Geographic restrictions
  on content.
· Basic tracking by websites
  (IP-based).
VPN in the Context of Internet Services
Service Description
VPN Routes all traffic through an encrypted server, hiding your
IP address and protecting your data on public networks.
Popular services: NordVPN, ProtonVPN, Mullvad.
Important · VPN Limitations
A VPN does NOT make you completely anonymous online. Your VPN provider can still
see your traffic. Always choose a trusted, no-logs VPN provider and understand
that VPNs are a privacy tool, not a shield for illegal activity.
Key Terms · Added
Term Definition

What This Means For Your Privacy:
· Your ISP can NOT see which websites you visit (only encrypted tunnel to VPN)
· Public Wi-Fi eavesdroppers see only encrypted data · useless to them
· Websites see the VPN server's IP, not your real location
· Your VPN provider CAN still see your traffic · choose a trusted no-logs provider

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
11.1  What is Email? 
Email (Electronic Mail) is a method of sending and receiving text messages and files digitally 
over the internet. Email is one of the oldest and most widely used internet services. It is 
faster, cheaper, and more flexible than postal mail. 
Feature Description 
Speed Delivered in seconds anywhere in the world. 
Cost Free to use (just requires internet connection). 
Attachments You can send files, photos, and documents. 
Access Can be read from any device with internet 
access. 
Storage Emails can be stored indefinitely for reference. 
 
11.2  How Email Works 
 
Figure 11.1 — How Email Works: From Compose to Inbox 
Protocol Role 
SMTP Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — used to SEND 
emails. 
POP3 Post Office Protocol v3 — downloads emails to 
device and removes from server.

emails across devices without removing from 
server.

Best Practices for Writing Emails 
• Use a clear, specific subject line (e.g., "Assignment Submission - Chapter 3", not just 
"Hi"). 
• Start with a greeting (Dear Mr. Ali, Hello Sarah). 
• Keep the message clear and concise — one main point per email. 
• Use proper grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

• Sign off professionally (Regards, Sincerely, Thank you). 
• Only attach files that are necessary. Compress large files. 
 
11.6  Managing Your Inbox 
Action Description

recipients. Use carefully.

11.7  Email Safety 
Phishing Warning — Stay Alert 
Phishing emails pretend to be from banks, delivery companies, or websites to trick you into 
entering your password or card details. 
Signs of phishing: urgent language ("Your account will be closed!"), spelling errors, 
suspicious sender address, links that look wrong. 
 
• Never open attachments from unknown senders — may contain viruses. 
• Do not click links in suspicious emails — phishing attacks steal your information. 
• Never share your email password with anyone. 
• Use a strong password and enable two-factor authentication (2FA). 
• Check the sender's address carefully — fake addresses mimic real ones.

body:
Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
12.1  Why Cyber Safety Matters 
As we spend more of our lives online — for study, communication, and entertainment — it is 
increasingly important to stay safe. Cyber threats can steal your personal data, damage your 
devices, harm your reputation, or put you in danger. Being a responsible digital citizen means 
knowing the risks and taking steps to protect yourself and others. 
 
12.2  Common Cyber Threats 
 
Figure 12.1 — Common Cyber Threats: Types and Descriptions 
Threat Description 
Virus A malicious program that attaches to files and 
spreads, corrupting or deleting data. 
Worm Similar to a virus but spreads across networks 
automatically without user action. 
Trojan Horse Disguises itself as legitimate software but 
secretly performs harmful actions. 
Ransomware Encrypts your files and demands payment to 
restore access. 
Spyware Secretly monitors your activity and sends data 
to a third party. 
Adware Displays unwanted adverts and may slow down 
your device. 
97

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Threat Description 
Phishing Fake emails, messages, or websites that trick 
you into giving personal information. 
Keylogger Records every keystroke to steal passwords 
and private information. 
DDoS Attack Overwhelms a server with traffic to shut down a 
website or service. 
 
12.3  Creating Strong Passwords 
 
Figure 12.2 — Password Strength Scale and Two-Factor Authentication 
Rules for a Strong Password 
• At least 12 characters long. 
• Combination of UPPERCASE, lowercase, numbers, and symbols. 
• Not a real word, your name, birthday, or "password123". 
• Different password for every account. 
• Use a passphrase: A string of random words (e.g., BlueMango$Rain7Tree). 
 
Weak Password Strong Password 
Password G!r9@Lp2#kT7 
12345678 BlueMango$Rain7Tree 
ahmed2010 aH!m3d&X0z#99qW 
mehrajwani mehraj#Y0u_N0T!really 
 
Password Managers & Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) 
A password manager stores all your passwords securely in an encrypted vault. You only 
need to remember one master password. Examples: Bitwarden, LastPass, 1Password. 
2FA adds an extra layer of security. Even if someone has your password, they also need a 
second proof of identity — usually a code sent to your phone or generated by an app. 
98

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
• Enable 2FA on all important accounts: email, social media, banking. 
• Methods: SMS code, authenticator app (Google Authenticator), physical security key. 
 
12.4  Safe Browsing Habits 
• Check for HTTPS and the padlock icon before entering personal information on a 
website. 
• Do not download software from unknown or untrusted websites. 
• Do not click pop-up ads — they may download malware. 
• Use a reputable antivirus program and keep it updated. 
• Keep your OS and browser updated — updates patch security vulnerabilities. 
• Use a VPN (Virtual Private Network) on public Wi-Fi to encrypt your traffic. 
• Log out of accounts when using shared or public computers. 
 
12.5  Protecting Your Privacy Online 
• Never share your full name, address, phone number, or school details with strangers 
online. 
• Review and limit app permissions — does that game really need your location? 
• Use privacy settings on social media to control who sees your content. 
• Be careful about what you post — once online, it is very hard to fully remove. 
 
The Digital Footprint 
A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind every time you use the internet — search 
history, social media posts, comments, photos, and purchases. This information can be seen by 
employers, schools, and strangers. 
Always think before you post. 
 
12.6  Cyberbullying 
Cyberbullying is the use of digital technology to harass, threaten, humiliate, or harm another 
person. It can happen via social media, messaging apps, online games, or email. 
Forms of Cyberbullying 
Form Description 
Harassment Sending repeated mean or threatening 
messages. 
Exclusion Deliberately leaving someone out of online 
groups. 
Impersonation Creating a fake profile pretending to be 
someone else. 
Outing Sharing someone's private information or 
photos without consent. 
Trolling Posting inflammatory content to provoke 
emotional responses. 
 
99

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
How to Respond to Cyberbullying 
• Do not respond to the bully — it often escalates things. 
• Take screenshots as evidence. 
• Block and report the person on the platform. 
• Tell a trusted adult: parent, teacher, or school counsellor. 
• Contact the platform's safety team if the content is dangerous. 
 
12.7  Screen Time and Digital Wellbeing 
Too much screen time can affect your sleep, mental health, and physical wellbeing. Healthy 
digital habits include: 
• Set daily screen time limits and stick to them. 
• Avoid screens at least one hour before bedtime. 
• Take regular breaks: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 
seconds (20-20-20 rule). 
• Balance online and offline activities: sports, reading, social time. 
• Use apps like Screen Time (iOS) or Digital Wellbeing (Android) to monitor usage. 
 
12.8  Copyright and Intellectual Property 
Copyright protects original creative works — books, music, software, images, and videos. 
Using someone else's work without permission is illegal and unethical. 
• Cite sources when using information from websites in your work. 
• Use Creative Commons licensed images for school projects (check licence terms). 
• Do not download pirated software, music, or films. 
• If creating content, you automatically hold copyright over your own original work. 
  
100

12.2a  Social Engineering
While technical attacks like viruses and ransomware exploit weaknesses in software,
social engineering attacks exploit weaknesses in people. A social engineer
manipulates a victim into revealing confidential information or performing an action
that helps the attacker · no hacking required. Social engineering is responsible for
the majority of successful cyberattacks worldwide.
Types of Social Engineering Attacks
Attack Type How It Works
Phishing Fake emails pretending to be trusted organisations to steal
credentials. (Covered in detail in §11.7 and §12.2)
Vishing (Voice
Phishing)
Attacker calls by phone pretending to be bank, IT support, or
government. Pressures victim to reveal passwords or transfer
money.
Smishing (SMS
Phishing)
Fake text messages with malicious links. Common format: 'Your
parcel could not be delivered · click here to reschedule.'
Pretexting Attacker creates a fabricated scenario (pretext) to gain
trust. Example: 'I'm from IT · I need your password to fix
your account.'
Baiting Leaving infected USB drives in car parks or offices. Curiosity
leads victims to plug them in, installing malware
automatically.
Tailgating
(Piggybacking)
Physically following an authorised person through a secure
door without using a badge. Exploits politeness · 'Can you
hold the door?'
Quid Pro Quo Offering something in exchange for information. Example: fake
IT helpdesk offering to fix a problem in exchange for login
credentials.
Watering Hole Infecting a website frequently visited by the target group.
When employees visit, malware is silently installed on their
device.
The Golden Rule of Social Engineering Defence
Verify before you trust. Legitimate organisations will NEVER:
   · Ask for your password by phone, email, or chat
   · Pressure you to act immediately without time to think
   · Ask you to bypass security procedures 'just this once'
If in doubt, hang up / ignore the message and call back on an official number.
Key Terms · Added
Term Definition
Social Engineering Manipulating people psychologically to gain access or
information.
Vishing Voice phishing · social engineering via phone calls.
Smishing SMS phishing · social engineering via text messages.
Pretexting Creating a false scenario to manipulate a victim into
compliance.
Tailgating Physically following authorised personnel through a secure
door.

CHAPTER 13 
Logical Thinking and Problem 
Solving 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to: 
• Understand what computational thinking means 
• Apply decomposition to break problems into smaller parts 
• Use pattern recognition to identify similarities 
• Create abstractions to simplify problems 
• Follow a structured problem-solving process 
• Apply logical thinking to everyday situations 
  
103

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
13.1  What is Logical Thinking? 
Logical thinking means reasoning in a clear, step-by-step way to solve a problem or reach a 
conclusion. It involves identifying facts, spotting patterns, and making decisions based on 
evidence rather than guesswork. 
Computers are logical machines — they follow instructions exactly. To program a computer 
effectively, you must think logically and clearly. This skill is useful not just in computing but in 
everyday life: deciding what to do, solving puzzles, planning tasks. 
 
13.2  Computational Thinking 
Computational thinking is a problem-solving approach used by computer scientists. It has 
four key pillars that together provide a complete framework for tackling any complex problem. 
 
 
Figure 13.1 — The Four Pillars of Computational Thinking 
 
Pillar Description 
Decomposition Breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, 
more manageable sub-problems. 
Pattern Recognition Identifying similarities, trends, or repeating 
patterns within or between problems. 
Abstraction Focusing on the important details and ignoring 
irrelevant information. 
Algorithm Design Creating a clear, step-by-step solution to solve 
the problem or sub-problem. 
 
13.2.1  Decomposition 
When you face a large problem, it is overwhelming to try to solve it all at once. 
Decomposition means splitting it into smaller pieces, each of which is easier to understand 
and solve.

chapters.title: Pages 105–112
body:
Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Example: Planning a School Event 
Big problem: Organise a school sports day. Decompose it into: 
1. Book the venue 
2. Create a schedule of events 
3. Invite participants and form teams 
4. Arrange equipment 
5. Plan refreshments 
6. Set up safety procedures 
Each sub-task is now much easier to manage independently. 
 
13.2.2  Pattern Recognition 
Patterns are repeated ideas, structures, or sequences. Recognising patterns helps you solve 
problems faster because a solution that worked before may work again. 
• Example: If you can tie a shoelace, you can tie a bow on a gift box — same pattern. 
• In programming: A loop is used when you recognise a pattern of repeated actions. 
• In data: You recognise a pattern that temperatures are higher in summer every year. 
 
13.2.3  Abstraction 
Abstraction means simplifying a problem by hiding unnecessary details and only focusing on 
what matters. 
• A map is an abstraction of the real world — it shows roads and landmarks, not every 
blade of grass. 
• A school timetable is an abstraction — it shows subject names and times, not how 
each lesson is structured. 
• In programming: Using a function called printScore() is an abstraction — you do not 
need to know how it works, just that it prints the score. 
 
13.2.4  Algorithm Design 
An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. Good 
algorithms are: 
Property Description 
Finite Must have a clear start and end — cannot run forever. 
Unambiguous Each step is clear and cannot be misinterpreted. 
Effective They solve the problem correctly for all valid inputs. 
Efficient They solve the problem without unnecessary steps. 
 
 
 
105

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
13.3  Problem-Solving Process 
A structured approach to solving problems ensures nothing is missed. Follow these eight 
steps: 
Step Action 
1. 
Understand 
Read carefully. What is given? What is needed? 
2. 
Decompose 
Break the problem into smaller parts. 
3. Identify 
Patterns 
Have you seen something similar before? 
4. 
Abstraction 
What details are important? What can be ignored? 
5. Plan 
(Algorithm) 
Write out the steps needed to solve the problem. 
6. 
Implement 
Code it or carry it out. 
7. Test Does the solution work for all cases, including edge cases? 
8. Refine If it does not work perfectly, adjust and try again. 
 
13.4  Logic and Boolean Thinking 
Boolean logic uses only two values: TRUE and FALSE. Computers use Boolean logic in all 
decision-making. 
 
 
Figure 13.2 — Boolean Logic: AND, OR, NOT Truth Tables 
Operator Meaning and Example 
AND Both conditions must be true. Example: "Is it 
raining AND cold?" — only TRUE if both are 
true. 
OR At least one condition must be true. Example: 
"Is it raining OR cold?" — TRUE if either is true. 
106

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Operator Meaning and Example 
NOT Reverses the truth value. Example: "NOT 
raining" — TRUE if it is NOT raining. 
 
13.5  Sequence, Selection, and Iteration 
 
Figure 13.3 — The Three Fundamental Programming Constructs 
Construct Description 
Sequence Instructions are followed one after another, in 
order. Step 1, then Step 2, then Step 3... 
Selection (Decision) A condition is checked and different paths are 
followed depending on TRUE or FALSE. 
(IF/ELSE) 
Iteration (Loop) A set of instructions is repeated — either a set 
number of times (FOR loop) or while a 
condition is true (WHILE loop). 
 
Everyday Example: Making Tea 
SEQUENCE:  Boil water → Add teabag → Pour water → Add milk → Remove teabag. 
SELECTION:  IF you want sugar, add sugar. ELSE don't add sugar. 
ITERATION:  WHILE tea is too hot, wait. Then drink.

CHAPTER 14 
Algorithms 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to: 
• Define an algorithm and identify its key properties 
• Write algorithms in pseudocode 
• Trace through algorithms and predict outputs 
• Understand common searching and sorting algorithms 
• Evaluate algorithms for efficiency 
• Express algorithms in different forms 
  
109

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
14.1  What is an Algorithm? 
An algorithm is a precise, finite, step-by-step set of instructions designed to solve a specific 
problem or accomplish a task. Algorithms exist everywhere in life — a recipe, a bus 
timetable, a traffic signal sequence — but in computing, algorithms are the heart of every 
program ever written. 
 
Property Description 
Finite Must have a clear start and end — cannot run 
forever. 
Definite / Unambiguous Every step must be precise — no room for 
interpretation. 
Input Has zero or more inputs (data given to the 
algorithm). 
Output Produces one or more results. 
Effective Each step is basic enough to be carried out and 
actually solves the problem. 
Efficient Solves the problem in a reasonable number of 
steps, not wastefully. 
 
14.2  Ways to Express Algorithms 
14.2.1  Natural Language 
Writing the steps in plain English. Easy to understand but can be ambiguous. 
Example: Finding the Largest of Two Numbers 
1. Get number A from the user. 
2. Get number B from the user. 
3. If A is greater than B, then the largest is A. 
4. Otherwise, the largest is B. 
5. Display the largest number. 
 
14.2.2  Pseudocode 
Pseudocode is a simplified, code-like notation that describes an algorithm using structured 
language. It is not actual code — it cannot be run — but it closely resembles the structure of 
real programming code. It is used to plan before writing actual code. 
Pseudocode: Find Largest of Two Numbers 
INPUT A 
INPUT B 
IF A > B THEN 
    OUTPUT "A is largest" 
110

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
ELSE 
    OUTPUT "B is largest" 
ENDIF 
 
14.3  Pseudocode Conventions 
Construct Pseudocode Syntax 
Input INPUT variableName 
Output OUTPUT message or variable 
Assignment variable <- value  (or  variable = value) 
Selection (IF) IF condition THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF 
Count-controlled loop FOR i <- 1 TO 10 ... ENDFOR 
Condition loop WHILE condition DO ... ENDWHILE 
Repeat until REPEAT ... UNTIL condition 
 
14.4  Tracing an Algorithm 
Tracing means manually working through an algorithm step by step, tracking the value of 
each variable. This is used to check an algorithm is correct before coding it. 
Trace Table Example — Sum Numbers 1 to 5 
Algorithm:  total <- 0  |  FOR i <- 1 TO 5  |  total <- total + i  |  
ENDFOR  |  OUTPUT total 
Trace:  i=1: total=1  →  i=2: total=3  →  i=3: total=6  →  i=4: total=10  →  i=5: total=15  →  
Output: 15 
 
14.5  Common Algorithms 
111

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
 
Figure 14.1 — Linear Search vs Binary Search: Step-by-Step Comparison 
 
14.5.1  Linear Search 
Linear search looks at each item one by one from the beginning until the target is found or 
the list ends. 
• Best case: item is first — 1 comparison. 
• Worst case: item is last or missing — n comparisons. 
• Works on unsorted and sorted lists. 
 
14.5.2  Binary Search 
Binary search works only on sorted lists. It checks the middle item, then eliminates half the 
list with each comparison — making it far more efficient for large sorted lists. 
• Far more efficient than linear search for large sorted lists. 
• Each step halves the search space — very fast. 
• Requires the list to be sorted first. 
 
14.5.3  Bubble Sort

Figure 14.2 — Bubble Sort: Step-by-Step on [5, 3, 8, 1, 4] 
Bubble sort repeatedly steps through a list, compares adjacent items, and swaps them if they

Algorithm Description 
Bubble Sort Simple to understand, slow for large lists. Good 
for teaching. 
Insertion Sort Efficient for small or nearly sorted lists. 
Merge Sort Efficient for large lists but uses more memory. 
Quick Sort Very fast on average, used in real-world 
applications. 
 
14.6  Algorithm Efficiency

Figure 14.3 — Big-O Notation: How Efficiency Changes with Input Size 
Notation Meaning 
O(1) Constant time — speed does not change with 
input size. 
O(log n) Logarithmic — very efficient (e.g., binary 
search). Halves the problem each step. 
O(n) Linear time — speed grows proportionally with 
input (e.g., linear search). 
O(n log n) Log-linear — efficient for large inputs (e.g., 
merge sort). 
O(n²) Quadratic — slow for large inputs (e.g., bubble 
sort).

CHAPTER 15 
Flowcharts 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to: 
• Understand what a flowchart is and why it is used 
• Identify and use standard flowchart symbols correctly 
• Draw flowcharts for sequence, selection, and iteration 
• Convert between pseudocode and flowcharts

116

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
15.1  What is a Flowchart? 
A flowchart is a visual diagram that uses standard symbols connected by arrows to represent 
the steps and decisions in a process or algorithm. Flowcharts make it easy to visualise the 
logic of a program before coding it, and are used to communicate algorithms to others 
clearly. 
Flowcharts are used in computing, engineering, business process design, science, and 
education. 
 
15.2  Standard Flowchart Symbols 
 
Figure 15.1 — Standard Flowchart Symbols Reference Sheet 
Symbol Name Shape and Use 
Terminator (Start/End) Oval / Rounded rectangle. Used at the START 
and END of every flowchart. Every flowchart 
must have exactly one START and at least one 
END. 
Process Rectangle. Represents an action or instruction 
— calculating, assigning, or doing something. 
Example: total = total + score 
Decision Diamond / Rhombus. Represents a YES/NO or 
TRUE/FALSE question. Always has two exit 
arrows labelled Yes/No or True/False. 
Input / Output Parallelogram. Represents data entering 
(INPUT) or leaving (OUTPUT) the process. 
Flow Arrows Arrows. Connect symbols and show the 
direction of flow. 
Connector Small circle with a letter. Used when the 
flowchart continues on another page to avoid 
117

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Symbol Name Shape and Use 
crossing arrows. 
Predefined Process Rectangle with double vertical lines. 
Represents a sub-routine or function defined 
elsewhere. 
 
15.3  Rules for Drawing Flowcharts 
• Every flowchart must start with a START terminator. 
• Every flowchart must end with an END terminator (may be multiple END symbols). 
• All arrows must flow in the same general direction (usually top to bottom). 
• Decision diamonds always have exactly two exit paths (Yes/No). 
• Arrows must not cross each other if possible. 
• Each symbol should have one entry point (except START). 
• Use consistent, neat shapes of the same size. 
 
15.4  Flowchart Examples 
Example 1: Sequence — Calculate Area of a Rectangle 
This is a pure sequence — no decisions or loops. Steps are followed one after another: 
START → INPUT length → INPUT width → area = length × width [Process] → OUTPUT 
area → END. 
 
Example 2: Selection — Check if Number is Positive or Negative 
The decision diamond has two exit paths: Yes (number is positive → OUTPUT "Positive") 
and No (number is not positive → OUTPUT "Negative or Zero"). Both paths lead to END. 
 
Example 3: Iteration — Print Numbers 1 to 5 
The loop arrow goes back up to the decision, repeating the process until counter exceeds 5. 
START → counter = 1 → Is counter ≤ 5? → Yes: OUTPUT counter, counter = counter + 1, 
loop back → No: END. 
 
Example 4: Combined — Login System (Full Flowchart) 
118

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
 
Figure 15.2 — Complete Flowchart: Login System with 3-Attempt Limit 
 
15.5  Converting Between Pseudocode and 
Flowchart 
119

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
 
Figure 15.3 — Pseudocode to Flowchart Conversion Reference 
Pseudocode Construct Flowchart Equivalent 
INPUT x Parallelogram with "INPUT x" 
OUTPUT result Parallelogram with "OUTPUT result" 
total = total + 1 Rectangle with "total = total + 1" 
IF x > 0 THEN ... ELSE ... Diamond with "x > 0?" and two branches 
(Yes/No) 
FOR i = 1 TO 10 Diamond with "i <= 10?" and loop-back arrow 
WHILE count > 0 Diamond with "count > 0?" and loop-back arrow 
 
15.6  Tracing a Flowchart 
Tracing a flowchart means following its arrows step by step for a given input to determine the 
output. Use a trace table to record variable values at each step. 
Trace Example: Add numbers while sum < 20 
Flowchart: START → sum=0 → INPUT number → sum = sum + number → Is sum < 20? 
YES→loop  NO→OUTPUT sum → END 
Input: 7, 8, 6  →  Trace: sum=0 → sum=7 (7<20, loop) → sum=15 (15<20, loop) → sum=21 
(21≥20, stop)  →  Output: 21 
 
15.7  Flowchart Tools 
Tool Description 
Paper and Pencil Most important for exams — practice drawing 
by hand with a ruler. 
Microsoft Word / PowerPoint Insert > Shapes — flowchart shapes built in. 
Easy for school work.

CHAPTER 16 
Introduction to Coding (Scratch) 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to: 
• Understand what Scratch is and why it is used for learning coding 
• Navigate the Scratch interface 
• Create sprites and use backdrops 
• Use motion, looks, sound, and control blocks

123

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
16.1  What is Scratch? 
Scratch is a free, visual block-based programming language developed by the MIT Media 
Lab. Instead of typing code, beginners drag and snap together coloured blocks that represent 
programming instructions. This makes coding accessible to young learners without needing 
to worry about syntax errors. 
Scratch is used worldwide in schools to introduce programming concepts including 
sequences, loops, conditionals, variables, and events. Projects include animations, 
interactive stories, quizzes, and games. Scratch is available at scratch.mit.edu — free to use 
in any browser. 
 
16.2  The Scratch Interface 
 
Figure 16.1 — The Scratch Interface: Key Areas and Panels 
Area Description 
Stage (top right) The screen where your project runs. Shows 
sprites and backgrounds. 
Sprite List (bottom right) All sprites in your project. Click a sprite to 
select and edit it. 
Block Categories (left) Coloured categories: Motion, Looks, Sound, 
Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables, 
My Blocks. 
Block Palette (centre-left) Shows available blocks for the selected 
category. 
Scripts / Code Area (centre) Where you drag and assemble blocks to create 
scripts. 
Costume Tab Edit how a sprite looks. Each sprite can have 
multiple costumes. 
Sounds Tab Add and record sounds for your sprites. 
124

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Area Description 
Green Flag / Red Stop Green flag runs the project. Red stop sign 
stops it. 
 
16.3  Key Concepts in Scratch 
16.3.1  Sprites 
A sprite is a character or object in your Scratch project. The default sprite is the Scratch Cat. 
You can: 
• Choose from the Scratch library (hundreds of characters and objects). 
• Upload your own image. 
• Draw your own using the built-in paint editor. 
• Use a photo from your camera. 
 
16.3.2  Backdrops 
A backdrop is the background image on the Stage. Each project can have multiple backdrops 
— switching between them creates scene changes. Choose from library, draw, or upload. 
16.3.3  Costumes 
A sprite can have multiple costumes — different images that represent different states (e.g., 
walking frames). Switching between costumes quickly creates animation. 
 
16.4  Block Categories 
 
Figure 16.2 — Scratch Block Categories: What Each Colour Does 
Category (Colour) What it Does 
Motion (Blue) Move, turn, glide, and set position/direction of a 
sprite. 
Looks (Purple) Change costumes, size, colour effects. 
125

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Category (Colour) What it Does 
Show/hide sprites. Say or think text. 
Sound (Pink) Play sounds and music. Set volume and pitch. 
Events (Yellow) Triggers — when green flag clicked, when key 
pressed, when sprite clicked. 
Control (Orange) Wait, repeat, forever, if/else, stop, create clone. 
Loops and conditionals. 
Sensing (Light Blue) Detect if sprite is touching something, ask the 
user a question, use mouse/keyboard. 
Operators (Green) Maths: +, -, *, /. Comparisons: >, <, =. Logic: 
AND, OR, NOT. 
Variables (Dark Orange) Create, set, change, and show/hide variables. 
Create lists. 
My Blocks (Red) Create custom blocks (functions/procedures). 
 
16.5  Building Your First Projects 
Project 1: Make the Cat Move 
Script: Cat moves 10 steps when arrow key pressed 
when [right arrow] key pressed  →  [Events: yellow] 
move 10 steps  →  [Motion: blue] 
Repeat for all four arrow keys to move in all directions. 
 
Project 2: Simple Walking Animation 
Script: Walking animation with costume switching 
when green flag clicked  →  [Events] 
forever  →  [Control: orange loop]

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
17.1  What is Python? 
Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van 
Rossum, first released in 1991. It is famous for its clean, readable syntax that resembles 
plain English, making it one of the best languages for beginners. 
 
Why Python? Where Python is Used 
Easy to read and write Web development (Django, Flask) 
Free and open source Data science and machine learning 
Huge community and libraries Artificial intelligence and deep learning 
Works on all platforms Automation and scripting 
Versatile — from beginner to expert Scientific research and education 
 
Setting Up Python 
• Download: python.org — download the latest version for your OS. 
• IDLE: Python's built-in editor — simple and good for beginners. 
• Thonny: Beginner-friendly Python IDE with built-in debugger. 
• Online: replit.com or onlinegdb.com — run Python in your browser, no installation 
needed.

intermediate learners. 
 
17.2  Your First Python Program 
# This is a comment -- Python ignores it 
print('Hello, World!') 
 
# Output: Hello, World! 
Figure 17.1 — Every Python journey begins with Hello, World! 
print() is a built-in function that outputs text to the screen. Text must be enclosed in quotes 
(single or double). Comments start with # and are ignored by Python — use them to explain 
your code. 
 
17.3  Variables and Data Types 
A variable is a named container that stores a value. In Python, you create a variable simply 
by assigning it a value — no need to declare its type first. 
 
131

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
 
Figure 17.2 — Python Data Types: str, int, float, bool, and list 
 
name       = 'Ahmed'    # str   (String — text) 
age        = 14         # int   (Integer — whole number) 
height     = 1.65       # float (Float — decimal number)

Operator Type Operators and Examples 
Arithmetic + (add)  - (subtract)  * (multiply)  / (divide)  // 
(floor divide)  % (modulo)  ** (power) Example:

Assignment = (assign)  += (add and assign)  -= (subtract

17.7  Iteration — Loops 
For Loop (Count-Controlled) 
# Print numbers 1 to 5

# range(5)         generates: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 
# range(0, 10, 2)  generates: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8  (step = 2)

17.9  Lists 
A list stores multiple values in a single variable, in order. Lists can contain any data type and 
can be changed (they are mutable). 
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

print(fruits[0])    # apple 
print(fruits[-1])   # cherry (last item)

fruits.append('mango')   # adds to end

17.10  A Complete Python Program 
Mini Grade Calculator — putting it all together 
# Grade Calculator Program 
 
def get_grade(mark): 
    if mark >= 90: return "A" 
    elif mark >= 75: return "B" 
    elif mark >= 60: return "C" 
    elif mark >= 50: return "D" 
    else: return "F" 
 
name  = input("Enter student name: ") 
marks = [] 
 
for subject in range(3): 
    m = int(input(f"Enter mark for subject {subject + 1}: ")) 
    marks.append(m) 
 
average = sum(marks) / len(marks) 
grade   = get_grade(average) 
 
print(f"Student: {name}") 
print(f"Average: {average:.1f}") 
print(f"Grade:   {grade}")

17.9a  Dictionaries
A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Unlike a list which uses numbered index
positions, a dictionary lets you label each value with a meaningful key.
Dictionaries are one of Python's most important and widely used data structures ·
used in APIs, databases, configuration files, and almost every real Python program.
# Create a dictionary
student = {
    'name':  'Ahmed',
    'age':   14,
    'grade': 'A'
}
# Access values by key
print(student['name'])      # Ahmed
print(student['grade'])     # A
# Add or update a key
student['subject'] = 'Maths'
student['age'] = 15          # updates existing key
# Delete a key
del student['subject']
# Check if a key exists
if 'name' in student:
    print('Name found!')
# Loop through key-value pairs
for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, ':', value)
Common Dictionary Methods
Method / Operation Description & Example
d[key] Access value: student['name'] · 'Ahmed'
d[key] = value Add or update: student['age'] = 15
del d[key] Delete a key-value pair
d.get(key) Safe access · returns None if key missing (no error)
d.keys() Returns all keys: dict_keys(['name', 'age', 'grade'])
d.values() Returns all values: dict_values(['Ahmed', 14, 'A'])
d.items() Returns key-value pairs for looping
len(d) Number of key-value pairs in the dictionary
key in d True/False · check if key exists
Lists vs Dictionaries · When to Use Which
Use a list when order matters and items are identified by position: scores = [85, 90, 78]
Use a dictionary when items are identified by a meaningful label: student = {'name':'Ahmed'}
Rule of thumb: if you find yourself writing list[0], list[1], list[2] with meaning, use a dict.

17.11  Error Handling · try / except
When a Python program encounters an unexpected situation · such as a user typing
text when a number is expected · it raises an exception and crashes. Error handling
lets you catch these exceptions and respond gracefully instead of crashing.
Basic Syntax:
try:
    age = int(input('Enter your age: '))
    print('You are', age, 'years old.')
except ValueError:
    print('Please enter a valid whole number.')
The try block contains the code that might cause an error. If an exception occurs,
Python jumps to the except block instead of crashing. Execution continues normally
after the except block.
Common Exception Types:
Exception When It Occurs
ValueError Wrong data type · e.g. int('hello')
ZeroDivisionError Division by zero · e.g. 10 / 0
IndexError List index out of range · e.g. lst[99] on a short list
FileNotFoundError Trying to open a file that does not exist
TypeError Wrong type for an operation · e.g. 'hello' + 5
Extended Example with Multiple Exceptions:
try:
    num   = int(input('Enter a number: '))
    result = 100 / num
    print('Result:', result)
except ValueError:
    print('That is not a valid number.')
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('Cannot divide by zero.')
finally:
    print('Program finished.')  # always runs
·  Common Python Mistakes · Beginners Should Watch Out For These
1. Forgetting int() or float() after input() · input() always returns a string.
2. Off-by-one in range() · range(1,6) gives 1,2,3,4,5 (not 6).
3. Incorrect indentation · Python uses 4 spaces; mixing tabs and spaces causes errors.
4. Using = instead of == in conditions · = assigns, == compares.
5. Mutable default arguments · avoid using lists as default function parameters.

CHAPTER 18 
Artificial Intelligence 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:

18.1  What is Artificial Intelligence? 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science concerned with creating systems 
that can perform tasks that would normally require human intelligence. These tasks include 
understanding language, recognising images, making decisions, solving problems, and 
learning from experience. 
The term "Artificial Intelligence" was coined by computer scientist John McCarthy in 1956. 
Today, AI is one of the most rapidly advancing fields in technology. 
 
Key Distinction: Intelligence vs Artificial Intelligence 
Intelligence: The ability to learn, reason, solve problems, and adapt. 
Artificial Intelligence: Machines that simulate aspects of human intelligence using 
algorithms and data. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
140

18.2  Types of AI 
 
Figure 18.1 — Types of AI: By Capability and By Approach 
 
18.2.1  Based on Capability 
Type Description 
Narrow AI (Weak AI) AI designed for one specific task. Cannot do 
anything outside its training. Examples: face 
recognition, spam filters, chess engines. ALL 
current AI is Narrow AI. 
General AI (Strong AI) Hypothetical AI that can perform any 
intellectual task a human can. Does NOT exist 
yet — it is a future goal.

intelligence in every domain. Does NOT exist 
— a theoretical concept for the far future.

Approach Description

systems. Example: simple chatbots with

and language.

18.3  Machine Learning 
Machine Learning (ML) is the most important technique in modern AI. Instead of writing rules 
manually, we feed an ML system data and it learns the rules by itself. 
 
18.3.1  How Machines Learn 
Step Action 
1. Collect 
Data

2. Choose

5.

18.3.3  Neural Networks and Deep Learning 
 
Figure 18.3 — Artificial Neural Network: Input → Hidden Layers → Output 
A neural network is a computing model inspired by the human brain. It is made up of layers 
of nodes (neurons) connected by weighted links. Data flows through input layers, hidden 
layers, and output layers. 
• Deep Learning: Neural networks with many hidden layers — extremely powerful for 
complex tasks. 
• Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): Specialised for image recognition.

Examples: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini.

CHAPTER 19 
Ethics of AI 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to: 
• Understand what AI ethics means and why it matters 
• Identify key ethical issues: bias, privacy, fairness, transparency 
• Discuss the social impact of AI on employment and society 
• Understand the concept of responsible AI 
• Evaluate AI decisions from an ethical perspective 
• Articulate personal views on the future of AI 
  
147

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
19.1  Why Ethics Matters in AI 
Artificial Intelligence is becoming part of nearly every aspect of modern life — from the videos 
recommended to you, to decisions about who gets a bank loan, to medical diagnosis. As AI 
becomes more powerful and widespread, the decisions it makes have real consequences for 
real people. 
AI ethics is the field that asks: How should AI be designed, deployed, and governed to 
ensure it is safe, fair, and beneficial for everyone? This is not just a question for engineers — 
it concerns all of us. 
 
Why Ethics Cannot Be Ignored 
AI systems have already been found to: 
• Wrongly identify innocent people as criminals (facial recognition bias) 
• Deny loans or jobs to people unfairly (biased training data) 
• Spread misinformation at scale (deepfake videos) 
• Make life-or-death decisions in autonomous weapons 
Getting AI ethics right is urgent and important. 
 
19.2  Key Principles of Ethical AI 
 
148

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Figure 19.1 — The Seven Principles of Ethical AI 
Principle Description 
Fairness AI systems should treat all people equally, 
regardless of race, gender, age, religion, or 
background. They should not discriminate. 
Transparency AI decisions should be explainable. People 
should be able to understand why an AI made 
a particular decision — especially in high-
stakes areas. 
Accountability When an AI system causes harm, there must 
be clear responsibility. Who is accountable — 
the developer, the company, the user? 
Privacy AI systems should collect and use only the data 
necessary for their purpose, and protect 
personal information. 
Safety AI must be tested thoroughly to ensure it does 
not cause harm, especially in critical systems 
like healthcare, transport, and military. 
Beneficence AI should be designed to benefit humanity, not 
just profit for companies. 
Human Oversight Humans must remain in control of important AI 
decisions, especially where life or rights are at 
stake. 
 
19.3  AI Bias 
AI bias occurs when an AI system produces unfair or discriminatory results. Bias usually 
enters AI through training data — if the data reflects historical inequalities, the AI will learn 
and perpetuate those inequalities. 
 
 
149

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
Figure 19.2 — AI Bias: How It Enters and Real-World Examples 
 
How to Reduce AI Bias 
• Use diverse, representative training data. 
• Audit AI systems regularly for discrimination. 
• Include diverse teams in AI development. 
• Test AI on edge cases and minority groups. 
• Make the decision-making process transparent and explainable. 
 
19.4  Privacy and Surveillance 
AI requires huge amounts of data — much of it personal. Ethical concerns around privacy 
include: 
• Data Collection: Apps and devices collect location, messages, purchases, and 
browsing history — often without users fully understanding what is shared. 
• Facial Recognition Surveillance: AI-powered CCTV cameras can identify individuals 
in public without their knowledge or consent — raising serious civil liberties concerns. 
• Profiling: AI can build detailed profiles of individuals to predict or influence behaviour. 
• Data Breaches: If personal data used to train AI is hacked, people's privacy is 
violated. 
 
GDPR — General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 
The EU's GDPR gives people rights over their personal data, including: the right to know what 
data is collected, the right to have it deleted, and the right not to be subject to fully automated 
decisions that significantly affect them. 
 
19.5  Deepfakes and Misinformation 
A deepfake is a highly realistic AI-generated image or video that makes it appear someone 
said or did something they did not. Deepfake technology uses deep learning (especially 
Generative Adversarial Networks — GANs) to produce convincing fake media. 
 
Risks of Deepfakes 
• Political misinformation: Fake videos of politicians saying things they never said. 
• Non-consensual intimate images: A serious form of online abuse and harassment. 
• Fraud: Fake audio of a CEO's voice used to trick companies into transferring money. 
• Eroding trust: When nothing can be trusted as genuine, public discourse suffers. 
 
Detecting Deepfakes 
• AI detection tools are being developed to identify deepfakes. 
• Look for: unnatural blinking, lighting inconsistencies, blurry edges around the face. 
• Verify sources — only trust media from reliable, verified organisations. 
 
19.6  AI and Employment 
150

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist 
 
 
 
Figure 19.3 — AI and Employment: Jobs at Risk vs New Jobs Created 
 
The Key Skill for the Future 
Humans working alongside AI — using creativity, emotional intelligence, and critical 
thinking that machines cannot replicate. 
 
19.7  Autonomous Weapons and AI in Warfare 
Lethal Autonomous Weapons (LAWs) — sometimes called "killer robots" — are weapons 
that can identify and attack targets without human input. This raises profound ethical 
questions: 
• Can a machine make a morally justified decision to take a human life? 
• Who is responsible if an autonomous weapon kills a civilian by mistake? 
• Should there be an international ban on fully autonomous lethal weapons? 
Many AI researchers, ethicists, and human rights organisations argue that life-and-death 
decisions must always involve meaningful human control. 
 
19.8  Responsible AI Development 
Major organisations and governments are developing frameworks and principles for 
responsible AI. Key commitments include: 
• Human-centred design: AI should serve human needs and respect human rights. 
• Inclusive development: AI should not exclude or disadvantage marginalised groups. 
• Environmental responsibility: Large AI models have significant carbon footprints — 
sustainability matters. 
• International cooperation: AI governance cannot be left to one country or company. 
 
Organisation AI Ethics Initiative 
European Union AI Act (2024) — first comprehensive AI 
regulation law in the world. 
UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI — global 
151

Foundations of Computer Science: From Basics to AI | The Monotheist
19.8a Global AI Governance (Beyond the EU)
While the EU AI Act is the first comprehensive legal framework, many other nations
and organisations have developed significant AI governance initiatives.
Understanding the global landscape is essential for anyone working with AI at an
international level.
Organisation / Region AI Governance Initiative
United Kingdom AI Safety Institute (2023) · world's first government
AI safety body. Focuses on frontier AI risks and
coordinates international testing.
United States Executive Order on AI (2023) · requires safety testing
for powerful AI, protects privacy, and promotes
responsible innovation. NIST AI Risk Management
Framework provides voluntary guidance.
China Generative AI Regulations (2023) · requires AI-
generated content to be labelled, prevents AI from
undermining state authority, and mandates data security
reviews.
Canada Voluntary Code of Conduct on Generative AI (2023) ·
industry commitments on safety, transparency, and human
rights protections.
UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) · adopted by
all 193 UNESCO member states. Covers human rights,
transparency, and environmental sustainability.
G7 / GPAI Hiroshima AI Process (2023) and Global Partnership on
AI · international coordination on responsible AI
across leading democracies.
Key Insight · AI Governance is Global
No single country or region controls AI development. Effective governance requires
international cooperation to set shared standards on safety, transparency,
and human rights · just as aviation and nuclear safety require global frameworks.
As you study AI ethics, be aware that different countries may permit or restrict AI uses
differently. A system legal in one country may be banned in another. This complexity makes
understanding multiple governance frameworks increasingly important.

Chapter Review Questions 
A. Short Answer 
1. What is AI ethics? Why does it matter? 
2. What is AI bias? Give two real-world examples and explain their harm. 
3. What is a deepfake? What are three risks it poses to society? 
4. How is AI changing employment? Name three jobs at risk and three new jobs being 
created. 
5. What are the key principles of responsible AI? Name and explain four. 
 
B. Discussion Questions 
1. A hospital uses AI to decide which patients receive organ transplants. What ethical 
issues does this raise? Who should have the final decision? 
2. Should facial recognition cameras be used in public spaces by governments? Argue 
both for and against. 
3. Is it ethical for companies to use AI to screen job applicants? What safeguards should 
be required? 
 
C. True or False 
1. AI bias only occurs if the programmers are personally biased.  (True / False) 
2. Deepfakes are created using deep learning technology.  (True / False) 
3. The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive AI regulation law in the world.  (True / False) 
4. AI is expected to create no new jobs — only destroy existing ones.  (True / False) 
5. Human oversight of AI decisions is especially important in high-stakes areas.  (True / 
False) 
 
D. Key Terms Glossary 
Term Definition 
AI Ethics The study of moral principles guiding how AI is 
designed, used, and governed. 
AI Bias Unfair or discriminatory outputs from an AI 
system, usually caused by biased training data. 
Deepfake AI-generated realistic fake image or video 
making it appear someone did or said 
something false. 
Transparency The ability to explain and understand how an AI 
system reaches its decisions. 
Accountability Being responsible for the consequences of an 
AI system's actions or decisions. 
GDPR EU regulation giving individuals rights over their 
personal data. 
Autonomous Weapons Weapons that can identify and attack targets 
without human control. 
Responsible AI AI developed and deployed with fairness, 
safety, privacy, and human welfare in mind.
